chapter_theme: The last seven kannis of Kudhambai Siddhar keep the question 'what need of it?' but turn from ritual instruments to the household and the kitchen: adornment for one who has conquered Death, spice for one who has eaten pepper and ginger, coconut milk for one who drinks mango milk on the mountain, a veil for one who walks the town by day, a household shrine for one with no property or house, lingering desire for one who knows himself and has joined the Lord, and permission for the wife who stays with her husband and the Lord.
structure_note: The same three-line kanni as chapter 81. 1601 and 1602 are food riddles that tradition reads in cipher; 1603 and 1604 are the wanderer's homelessness; 1605 and 1606 close the song on union, the last playing on பதி as husband and Lord.

1600.reading: For the knowers of the true intent who have conquered Death, what need of adornments?
1600.nuance: கோலங்கள் covers dress, decoration and assumed forms, including the ascetic's costume; the one who has beaten காலன், Death, has no body left to dress for and no role to play.

1601.reading: Onion is eaten, pepper is eaten, dry ginger is eaten: what need of asafoetida to eat?
1601.nuance: The stanza turns on காயம், which is both asafoetida (as in பெருங்காயம்) and the body. On the plain reading it is a kitchen joke: with these three pungent things already eaten, the fourth adds nothing. On the coded reading tradition hears வெண்காயம் as the white or purified body and உண்காயம் as the body that eats, so that the one who has taken the Siddhars' medicines no longer needs a body fed in the common way. The line names medicinal staples; it gives no preparation.

1602.reading: For those who drink mango milk and sit on the mountain, what need of coconut milk?
1602.nuance: Plainly, the hermit on the hill lives on the sap of wild mango rather than the village's coconut milk. Tradition takes the mountain as the crown of the head and மாங்காய்ப்பால் as the nectar that flows there in yoga, against which ordinary food is nothing; the code is not explained in the verse.

1603.reading: For those who roam round the town in broad daylight, what need of a head-cloth to hide under?
1603.nuance: முட்டாக்கு is the cloth pulled over the head to avoid being recognised, or a woman's veil. The knower goes openly by day and has nothing to hide, from shame or from the world's eye.

1604.reading: One has no property and no house of one's own: what need of a household shrine?
1604.nuance: தாவரம் is immovable property; தேவாரம் is both the daily worship kept in a home (the shrine box and its rites) and the hymns of the Saiva saints. The homeless man has nowhere to keep the first; the second reading, a dismissal of the canonical hymns, is possible but harsher than the pairing with 'house' suggests.

1605.reading: For those who have known themselves and joined the Lord, what need of desire that comes after?
1605.nuance: பின்னாசை is desire that lingers or comes afterwards: once the self is known and the Lord reached, there is no further thing to want. The order is the Siddhars' usual one, self-knowledge first and then the Lord.

1606.reading: For those who stay with the husband and themselves with the Lord, what need of a word of permission?
1606.nuance: The stanza plays on பத்தா (husband) and பதி (husband, the Lord, or a dwelling). Addressed to a woman, it says plainly that the wife at home with her husband needs no one's leave; in the devotional reading the soul as bride, united with the Lord, needs no answer or sanction. உத்தாரம் may be permission, command or reply.

links.note: Tirumular calls pure Saivas those who go beyond outward garb to Siva's side without show; Kudhambai asks what adornments or guises are to those who have conquered Death. Both make the costume something the realised have left behind, Tirumular naming Siva as the goal, Kudhambai the victory over Death.

Tirumular tells of drinking the nectar that is milk at the upper place, reached by driving bindu and nada; Kudhambai sets mango milk on the mountain against coconut milk. Read in the coded way, the milk on the height is the same yogic nectar; Kudhambai leaves the code unstated.

Tirumular describes the teacher who cut through the heavens as a solitary man in this world with no house of his own; Kudhambai's knower has no property and no house, and so no household shrine. Tirumular makes homelessness the guru's mark, Kudhambai the reason household worship falls away.

Tirumular says that when one knows oneself and becomes one with Siva, malam and the gunas die and birth ends; Kudhambai says that for those who know themselves and join the Lord no desire remains. The sequence, self-knowledge then union, is the same; Tirumular counts the bonds that die, Kudhambai only the desire.

The Kural makes giving up craving the cause of an unshifting nature; Kudhambai makes the end of desire the consequence of knowing oneself and joining the Lord. The Kural asks for the renunciation first, Kudhambai expects it to follow.

source_issues: 1601: the pun on காயம் (asafoetida and body) means உண்காயம் has no settled sense; the word division is editorial.
1606: பத்தாவுந் தானும் பதியோடு allows several constructions (husband and self with the Lord, or husband and wife at home); the line may be compressed.
